# Associates
## Definition 1
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity, and let $a, b \in R$.

**(i)** If $b = ac$ for some $c \in R$, then we say that $a$ ***divides*** $b$, denoted by $a \vert b$. In this case, $a$ is called a ***factor*** (or ***divisor***) of $b$, and $b$ is called a ***multiple*** of $a$.

**(ii)** $a$ and $b$ are called ***associates*** in $R$ if $a \vert b$ and $b \vert a$.

**(iii)** $a$ and $b$ are called ***strongly associates*** in $R$ if $a = bu$ for some unit $u$ of $R$.

환에서는 곱셈이 정의되기에 정수론과 비슷한 센스로 약수, 배수와 같은 개념을 정의할 수 있다. 특별히 두 원소가 서로를 나누는 관계에 있는 경우 **associates**, 특별히 단위원에 대해서 관계가 있다면 **strongly associates**라고 부른다. 일반적으로 strongly associates이면 associate이지만, 역은 성립하지 않는다. 역 또한 성립하기 위해서는 주어진 환 $R$이 정역(Integral Domain)이면 가능함이 아래 Remark에 서술되어 있다. 

## Remark 1
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity, and let $a, b \in R$.

**(i)** $b \vert a \iff (a) \subset (b)$.

Divisible의 관계와 ideal의 포함 관계가 반대라고 생각하면 외우기 편하다.

**(ii)** $a$ and $b$ are associates $\iff$ $(a) = (b)$.

즉 $a$와 $b$가 associates라는 말은 두 원소가 생성하는 아이디얼 $(a)$와 $(b)$가 서로 같음을 의미한다.

**(iii)** The relation $\sim$ on $R$ defined by

$$a \sim b \iff a \text{ and } b \text{ are associates in } R$$

is an equivalence relation on $R$.

**(iv)** The relation $\approx$ on $R$ defined by

$$a \approx b \iff a \text{ and } b \text{ are strongly associates in } R$$

is an equivalence relation on $R$.

**(v)** If $a \approx b$, then $a \sim b$. However, the converse does not hold in general.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
If $a \approx b$, then $a = bu$ for some unit $u$ of $R$, so $b \vert a$. Since $u$ is a unit, we have $b = au^{-1}$, so $a \vert b$. Hence, $a \sim b$.

However, $a \sim b$ does not imply $a \approx b$. Here is the counterexample:

Consider the ring $\langle C[0, 1], +, \cdot \rangle$ of real-valued continuous functions on $[0, 1]$. Then $\langle C[0, 1], +, \cdot \rangle$ is a commutative ring with identity.

Let $f(x), g(x) \in C[0, 1]$ be given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases}
\frac{1}{3} - x & \left( 0 \le x < \frac{1}{3} \right) \\
0 & \left( \frac{1}{3} \le x < \frac{2}{3} \right) \\
x - \frac{2}{3} & \left( \frac{2}{3} \le x \le 1 \right)
\end{cases} \quad \text{and} \quad g(x) = \begin{cases}
f(x) & \left( 0 \le x \le \frac{1}{2} \right) \\
-f(x) & \left( \frac{1}{2} < x \le 1 \right).
\end{cases}$$

If $h(x) \in C[0, 1]$ is given by

$$h(x) = \begin{cases}
1 & \left( 0 \le x < \frac{1}{3} \right) \\
3 - 6x & \left( \frac{1}{3} \le x < \frac{2}{3} \right) \\
-1 & \left( \frac{2}{3} \le x \le 1 \right),
\end{cases}$$

then we have that $f(x) = g(x)h(x)$ and $g(x) = f(x)h(x)$, so $g(x) \vert f(x)$ and $f(x) \vert g(x)$. Hence, $f(x) \sim g(x)$. We will show that $f(x) \not \approx g(x)$.

Suppose that $f(x) \approx g(x)$. Then $f(x) = g(x)u(x)$ for some unit $u(x)$ of $C[0, 1]$. Note that $u(x) \neq 0, \forall x \in [0, 1]$.

Since $f(0) = g(0) = f(1) = \frac{1}{3}$ and $g(1) = -\frac{1}{3}$, we have $u(0) = 1$ and $u(1) = -1$. By the intermediate value theorem, $u(c) = 0$ for some $c \in (0, 1)$, which is a contradiction. Hence, $f(x) \not \approx g(x)$. $\blacksquare$
:::

**(vi)** If $R$ is an integral domain, then $a \sim b \iff a \approx b$.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
We only need to show that $a \sim b \implies a \approx b$.

If $a \sim b$, then $a \vert b$ and $b \vert a$, so $a = bc$ and $b = ad$ for some $c, d \in R$. Then $a = bc = (ad)c = adc$. Since $R$ is an integral domain, we have $1 = dc$, which means that $c$ is a unit. Hence, $a = bc$ implies that $a \approx b$. $\blacksquare$
:::

**(vii)** Let $c$ be an irreducible element of an integral domain $D$. If $c$ and $d$ are associates in $D$, then $d$ is also an irreducible element of $D$.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
Since $c$ is irreducible, $(c)$ is maximal among all proper principal ideals of $D$ by Theorem 1 **(i)**. Since $c$ and $d$ are associates, we have $(c) = (d)$, so $(d)$ is maximal among all proper principal ideals of $D$. Hence, $d$ is irreducible in $D$. $\blacksquare$
:::

# Irreducible, Prime
## Definition 2
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity.

**(i)** Let $c$ be a nonzero nonunit in $R$. Then $c$ called an ***irreducible element*** of $R$ if whenever $a, b \in R$ with $c = ab$, either $a$ or $b$ is a unit of $R$.

**(ii)** Let $p$ be a nonzero nonunit in $R$. Then $p$ is called a ***prime element*** of $R$ if whenever $a, b \in R$ with $p \vert ab$, either $p \vert a$ or $p \vert b$.

주의할 점은, **기약다항식(Irreducible Polynomial)**과 **기약원(Irreducible Element)**은 일반적으로 같은 개념이 아니다. 예를 들어 $\mathbb{Z}[x]$의 원소 $2x^2+2$를 생각해보면 이 다항식은 $\mathbb{Z}$에서 영점을 갖지 않으므로 $\mathbb{Z}[x]$의 기약다항식은 맞지만 $2x^2+2 = 2(x^2+1)$과 같이 $\mathbb{Z}[x]$의 단위원이 아닌 두 원소로 인수분해되므로 기약원은 아니다. 이는 $\mathbb{Z}$의 모든 원소가 단위원이 아니므로, 다시 말해 $\mathbb{Z}$가 체가 아니므로 생기는 일이다. 즉 다항식환에서는 기약원이면 기약다항식이 되지만 역은 성립하지 않으므로 기약다항식이 더 넓은 개념이라고 할 수 있겠다. 따라서 두 개념이 같아지는 조건으로는 다항식환 $R[x]$에서 $R$이 체가 되면 기약다항식과 기약원은 동일한 개념으로 볼 수 있다.

## Theorem 1
Let $D$ be an integral domain, and let $c$ and $p$ be nonzero elements in $D$.

**(i)** $c$ is an irreducible element in $D$ $\iff$ $(c)$ is an ideal of $D$ which is maximal among all proper principal ideals of $D$.

**(ii)** $p$ is a prime element in $D$ $\iff$ $(p)$ is a nonzero prime ideal of $D$.

**(iii)** Every prime element in $D$ is irreducible in $D$. However, the converse does not hold in general.

$D$가 PID라는 보장이 없으면 주아이디얼이 아닌 아이디얼도 존재할 수 있으므로 **(i)**에서 바로 극대 아이디얼이라고 보장할 수는 없다. 거꾸로 PID이면 극대 아이디얼이라는 따름정리가 바로 튀어나온다.

한편 **(i)**은 직관적으로도 쉽게 납득이 가능한 정리인데, $c$가 기약원이라는 말은 달리 말하면 $c$의 인수분해가 자명한 방법 밖에 없다고도 볼 수 있다. $c = ab$이면 $a$나 $b$ 둘 중 하나는 반드시 단위원이기 때문이다. 한편 $(c) \subsetneq (x)$인 어떤 원소 $x$가 존재하면 반드시 $x \vert a$가 되는데, $x \neq a$이므로 $x$의 존재성으로 $a$의 자명하지 않은 인수분해가 보장된다. 이러한 사실이 맥시멀이라는 성질로 이어지는 것이다.

**(iii)**은 소원소(prime element)이면 기약원(irreducible element)이지만, 일반적으로 역은 성립하지 않는다. 이는 원소들의 소인수분해가 유일하지 않을 수 있고, 이때 서로 관련이 없는 원소들끼리 나눌 수는 없기 때문이다.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
**(i)** $(\implies)$ Suppose that $c$ is irreducible in $D$. If $(c) = D$, then $c$ is a unit because it is nonzero, which is impossible. Hence $(c)$ is a proper ideal of $D$. 

If $(c) \subset (x) \subsetneq D$ for some $x \in D$, then $x \vert c$, so $c = xy$ for some $y \in D$. Since $c$ is irreducible, either $x$ or $y$ is a unit of $D$. If $x$ is a unit of $D$, then $(x) = D$ which is impossible. Hence, $y$ is a unit of $D$, so $c \approx x$. Then $c \sim x$ which is equivalent to $(c) = (x)$. Thus, $(c)$ is maximal among all proper principal ideals of $D$.

$(\impliedby)$ Suppose that $(c)$ is maximal among all proper principal ideals of $D$. Since $(c)$ is a proper ideal of $D$, $c$ is not a unit of $D$.

Suppose that $c = ab$ for some $a, b \in D$. Then $a \vert c$, so $(c) \subset (a)$. By assumption, we obtain $(a) = (c)$ or $(a) = D$. If $(a) = (c)$, then $c \vert a$, which means that $a = cd$ for some $d \in D$, so $c = ab = (cd)b = cbd$. Since $D$ is an integral domain, we have $1 = bd$, which means that $b$ is a unit of $D$. 

If $(a) = D$, then $a$ is a unit of $D$. Hence, in any cases, $c$ is irreducible in $D$.

**(ii)** $(\implies)$ Suppose that $p$ is a prime element in $D$. If $(p) = D$, then $p$ is a unit because it is nonzero, which is impossible. Hence, $(p) \subsetneq D$. Moreover, $(p)$ is nonzero beceause $p$ is nonzero.

If $ab \in (p)$, then $p \vert ab$. Since $p$ is a prime element, we have $p \vert a$ or $p \vert b$, which means that $(a) \subset (p)$ or $(b) \subset (p)$. Hence, $a \in (p)$ or $b \in (p)$, so $(p)$ is a prime ideal of $D$.

$(\impliedby)$ Suppose that $(p)$ is a nonzero prime ideal of $D$. Since $(p) \subsetneq D$, $p$ is nonunit, and it is nonzero.

If $p \vert ab$ for some $a, b \in D$, then $(ab) \subset (p)$, so $ab \in (p)$. Since $(p)$ is a prime ideal of $D$, we have $a \in (p)$ or $b \in (p)$, which means that $p \vert a$ or $p \vert b$. Hence, $p$ is a prime element in $D$.

**(iii)** Let $p$ be a prime element in $D$. Then $p$ is nonzero and nonunit in $D$. If $p = ab$ for some $a, b \in D$, then $p \vert a$ or $p \vert b$ because $p$ is a prime element in $D$. WLOG, we may assume that $p \vert a$, so $a = pc$ for some $c \in D$. Then $p = ab = (pc)b = pcb$, so $1 = cb$. Hence, $b$ is a unit of $D$, which means that $p$ is irreducible in $D$. 

However, the converse does not hold in general. Here is the counterexample:

Let $D = \{ a + b \sqrt{-5} \mid a, b \in \mathbb{Z} \}$. Note that $2$ is nonzero and nonunit in $D$. If $2 = (a+b\sqrt{-5})(x+y\sqrt{-5})$ for some $a, b, x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$, then we have $ax-5by = 2$ and $ay + bx = 0$. Note that

$$\begin{align*}
(2+5by)by &= (ax)(by) \\
&= (ay)(bx) \\
&= (-bx)(bx) \\
&= -(bx)^2 \le 0,
\end{align*}$$

so $-\frac{2}{5} \le by \le 0$. Since $by \in \mathbb{Z}$, $by = 0$ and $ax = 2$. Since $a, x \neq 0$, we have 

$$\begin{align*}
ay = -bx \\
\implies \frac{y}{x} = - \frac{b}{a},
\end{align*}$$

so $b = 0 = y$. Furthermore, we obtain that $a = \pm 1$ or $x = \pm 1$, which means that either $a+b\sqrt{-5}$ or $x+y\sqrt{-5}$ is a unit of $D$. Hence, $2$ is an irreducible element in $D$. 

Suppose that $2$ is a prime element in $D$. Note that $2 \cdot 3 = 6 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$. Then $2$ must divide either $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ or $1 - \sqrt{-5}$, which is impossible. Hence, $2$ is not a prime element in $D$. $\blacksquare$
:::

# PID
## Definition 3
Let $D$ be an integral domain. Then $D$ is called a ***principal ideal domain (PID)*** if every ideal of $D$ is principal.

정역에 대해서 정의를 했지만, 실제로 모든 아이디얼이 주 아이디얼이기 위해서 반드시 정역이 되어야 할 필요는 없다. 일반적으로 모든 아이디얼이 주 아이디얼인 환을 **주 아이디얼 환(principal ideal ring, PIR)**이라고 부른다. 예컨대 $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$는 $2(6\mathbb{Z}) = \{ 0, 2, 4 \}$와 $3(6\mathbb{Z}) = \{ 0, 3 \}$에 대해서 $2(6\mathbb{Z}) \cdot 3(6\mathbb{Z}) = 6(6\mathbb{Z}) = \{ 0 \} = 0(6\mathbb{Z})$이므로 정역이 아니지만 모든 아이디얼이 주 아이디얼임을 쉽게 확인할 수 있다.

## Example 1
**(i)** Since all ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ is of the form $n\mathbb{Z} = (n)$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, $\mathbb{Z}$ is a PID. In particular, if $I$ is a nonzero ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$, then $I = (n)$ for the smallest positive integer $n$ in $I$.

**(ii)** If $F$ is a field, then $F[x]$ is a PID. In particular, if $I$ is a nonzero ideal of $F[x]$, then $I = (f(x))$ for a nonzero element $f(x)$ of $I$ of minimal degree.

## Theorem 2
Let $D$ be a PID, and let $p$ be a nonzero element in $D$.

**(i)** $p$ is irreducible in $D$ $\iff$ $(p)$ is a maximal ideal of $D$.

**(ii)** $p$ is irreducible in $D$ $\iff$ $p$ is a prime element in $D$.

**(iii)** Let $a_1, \dots, a_n \in D$. If $p$ is irreducible in $D$ and $p$ divides $a_1 \cdots a_n$, then $p$ divides $a_i$ for some $i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$.

따라서 PID에서는 기약원(irreducible element)과 소원소(prime element)는 서로 동치의 개념이다. 이 사실을 이용해서 어떤 환이 PID가 아님을 보일 수도 있는데, 정리 1의 **(iii)** 증명에서 언급한 환 $D = \{ a + b \sqrt{-5} \mid a, b \in \mathbb{Z} \}$는 PID가 아니다. 앞서 $2$라는 원소가 기약원이지만 소원소는 아님을 증명했는데, 이러한 원소의 존재가 정리 2 **(ii)**의 반례가 되기 때문이다. 따라서 어떤 환이 PID가 아님을 보이기 위해 정의 그대로 주 아이디얼이 아닌 아이디얼이 있음을 보여도 되지만, 이와 같이 기약원이지만 소원소가 아닌 원소의 존재를 보여도 된다.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
**(i)** It directly comes from Theorem 1 **(i)**.

**(ii)** Since we have already shown the $(\impliedby)$ direction in Theorem 1 **(iii)**, we only need to show the $(\implies)$ direction.

Suppose that $p$ is irreducible in $D$. If $p \vert ab$ for some $a, b \in D$, then $ab \in (p)$. By **(i)**, $(p)$ is a maximal ideal of $D$. Then $(p)$ is also a prime ideal of $D$, so $a \in (p)$ or $b \in (p)$. Hence, $p \vert a$ or $p \vert b$, so $p$ is a prime element in $D$. 

**(iii)**

$\blacksquare$
:::

## Theorem 3
Let $D$ be an integral domain.

**(i)** $D$ is a field $\iff$ $D[x]$ is a PID.

**(ii)** Let $F$ be a field, and let $0 \neq p(x) \in F[x]$. Then $(p(x))$ is a maximal ideal of $F[x]$ $\iff$ $p(x)$ is irreducible over $F$.

**(ii)**는 정리 2 **(i)**의 따름정리로 바라볼 수 있다.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
**(i)** $(\implies)$ Suppose that $D$ is a field. Let $N \lhd D[x]$. If $N = \{ 0 \}$, then $N = (0)$ is a principal ideal. If $N \neq \{ 0 \}$, then $N$ contains a polynomial $p(x)$ with $\deg(p(x)) \ge 0$. Choose $p(x)$ with minimal degree in $N$. 

If $\deg(p(x)) = 0$, then $p(x) \in D$. Since $D$ is a field and $p(x) \neq 0$, $p(x)$ is a unit in $N$, which implies that $N = D[x] = (1)$. Hence, $N$ is a principal ideal of $D[x]$.

Suppose that $\deg(p(x)) \ge 1$. We will show that $N = (p(x))$. Since $N$ is an ideal of $D[x]$, we have $(p(x)) \subset N$. For the reverse inclusion, let $f(x) \in N$. By the division algorithm for a polynomial ring, there uniquely exist $q(x), r(x) \in D[x]$ such that $f(x) = q(x)p(x) + r(x)$ where $r(x) = 0$ or $0 \le \deg(r(x)) < \deg(p(x))$. 

Note that $f(x) \in N$ and $q(x)p(x) \in (p(x)) \subset N$, so $q(x)p(x) \in N$. Then $r(x) = f(x) - q(x)p(x) \in N$ Since $\deg(r(x)) < \deg(p(x))$ and $p(x)$ is a minimal degree polynomial in $D$, $r(x) = 0$. Hence, $f(x) = q(x)p(x) \in (p(x))$, and therefore $N \subset (p(x))$. Thus, $N = (p(x))$ is a principal ideal of $D[x]$. Consequently, $D[x]$ is a PID.

$(\impliedby)$ Suppose that $D[x]$ is a PID. Let $d$ be a nonzero element in $D$. Then the two-generated principal ideal $(d, x)$ is a principal ideal, so $(d, x) = (f(x))$ for some $f(x) \in D[x]$. 

Since $d \in (f(x))$, $d = f(x)g(x)$ for some $g(x) \in D[x]$. Since $D$ is an integral domain, we have $\deg(f(x)) + \deg(g(x)) = 0$, which means that $\deg(f(x)) = 0 = \deg(g(x))$. Then $f(x) \in D$, so we write $f(x) = a$ for some $a \in D$.

Since $x \in (f(x)) = (a)$, $x = ah(x)$ for some $h(x) \in D[x]$. By comparing the coefficients of $x$, we have $1 = ab$ for some $b \in D$. Then $a \neq 0$ and $a$ is a unit in $D$, which means that $(d, x) = (f(x)) = (a) = D[x]$.

For $1 \in D[x]$, $1 = du(x) + xv(x)$ for some $u(x), v(x) \in D[x]$. Then $1 = du(0)$, which means that $d \neq 0$ and $d$ is a unit. Hence, $D$ is a field.

**(ii)** $(\implies)$ Suppose that $(p(x))$ is a maximal ideal of $F[x]$. Then $(0) \subsetneq (p(x)) \subsetneq F[x]$, so $p(x) \notin F$ because if $p(x) \in F$, then $p(x)$ is a unit, which implies that $(p(x)) = F[x]$. 

Suppose that $p(x) = f(x)g(x)$ for some $f(x), g(x) \in F[x]$. Then $f(x)g(x) \in (p(x))$, which implies that $f(x) \in (p(x))$ or $g(x) \in (p(x))$ because $(p(x))$ is a maximal ideal, so it is a prime ideal. Hence $\deg(p(x)) \le \deg(f(x))$ or $\deg(p(x)) \le \deg(g(x))$. Since $f(x)g(x) = p(x)$ and $F[x]$ is an integral domain, we have $\deg(p(x)) = \deg(f(x)) + \deg(g(x))$. Thus, $\deg(f(x)) = 0$ or $\deg(g(x)) = 0$, so $f(x) \in F$ or $g(x) \in F$. Consequently, $p(x)$ is irreducible over $F$.

$(\impliedby)$ Suppose that $p(x)$ is irreducible over $F$. Let $N$ be an ideal of $F[x]$ such that $(p(x)) \subset N \subset F[x]$. By **(i)**, $F[x]$ is a PID, so $N$ is a principal ideal of $F[x]$. Write $N = (f(x))$ for some $f(x) \in F[x]$. Since $p(x) \in N = (f(x))$, $p(x) = f(x)g(x)$ for some $g(x) \in F[x]$. Since $p(x)$ is irreducible over $F$, $\deg(f(x)) = 0$ or $\deg(g(x)) = 0$, which means that $f(x) \in F$ or $g(x) \in F$.

If $f(x) \in F$, then $f(x)$ is a unit, so $N = (f(x)) = F[x]$.

If $g(x) \in F$, then $g(x) = c$ for some $c \in F$. Then $p(x) = cf(x)$,s so $f(x) = \frac{1}{c} p(x) \in (p(x))$. Hence, $N = (f(x)) = (p(x))$. Consequently, $(p(x))$ is a maximal ideal of $F[x]$. $\blacksquare$
:::

## Example 2
**(i)** Let $f(x) = x^3 + 3x + 2 \in \mathbb{Z}_5[x]$. Since $f(0) = 2, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 1, f(3) = 3, f(4) = 3$, $f(x)$ does not have a zero in $\mathbb{Z}_5[x]$. Then $f(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_5$. By Theorem 7 **(ii)**, $(x^3 + 3x + 2)$ is a maximal ideal of $\mathbb{Z}_5[x]$. Then $\mathbb{Z}_5[x]/(x^3+3x+2)$ is a field.

**(ii)** Let $g(x) = x^2 - 2 \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$. Since $g(x)$ does not have a zero in $\mathbb{Q}$, it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then $(x^2 - 2)$ is a maximal ideal of $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ by Theorem 7 **(ii)**. Then $\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x^2-2)$ is a field.

# Noetherian Ring
## Definition 4
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity. Then $R$ is a ***Noetherian ring*** if every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated. If $R$ is a Noetherian ring and an integral domain, we call $R$ a ***Noetherian domain***.

## Example 3
**(i)**

## Theorem 4
**(i)** Every PID is a Noetherian domain.

**(ii)** **(Hilbert Basis Theorem)** If $R$ is a Noetherian ring, then $R[x]$ is a Noetherian ring. 

**(iii)** Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $\{ I_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ be an ascending chain of ideals of $R$, and let $\displaystyle I = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty I_n$. Then $I$ is an ideal of $R$.

**(iv)** Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity. TFAE

1. $R$ is a Noetherian ring.

2. $R$ satisfies the ***ascending chain condition*** of ideals, i.e., if $\{ I_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ is an ascending chain of ideals of $R$, then there is $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $I_n = I_N, \forall n \ge N$.

3. Every nonempty set of ideals of $R$ has a maximal element with respect to inclusion.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
:::

# UFD
## Definition 5
An integral domain $D$ is called a ***unique factorization domain (UFD)*** if the following conditions are satisfied:

**(i)** Every nonzero nonunit element of $D$ can be factored into a finite product of irreducible elements in $D$.

**(ii)** If $p_1 \cdots p_r$ and $q_1 \cdots q_s$ are two factorizations of the same element if $D$ into irreducible elements, then $r=s$ and there is some renumbering of the factors so that $p_i \approx q_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, r \}$.

## Example 3

## Theorem 5
**(i)** Every PID is a UFD.

**(ii)** **(Fundamental Theorem of Arithemetric)** $\mathbb{Z}$ is a UFD.

**(iii)** Let $D$ be a UFD. Then $p$ is irreducible in $D$ $\iff$ $p$ is prime in $D$.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
**(i)**

**(ii)** Since $\mathbb{Z}$ is a PID, it is a UFD by **(i)**.

**(iii)**
:::

# gcd
## Definition 6
- Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity, and let $a_1, \dots, a_n, d \in R \setminus \{ 0 \}$.

**(i)** $d$ is called a ***common divisor*** of $a_1, \dots, a_n$ if $d \vert a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$.  

**(ii)** $d$ is called a ***greatest common divisor (gcd)*** of $a_1, \dots, a_n$, denoted by $\gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)$, if it satisfies the following conditions:

1. $d$ is a common divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$.

2. If $r \in R$ is a common divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$, then $r \vert d$.

- Let $D$ be a UFD, and let $f(x) = a_0 + \cdots + a_nx^n$ be a nonzero polynomial in $D[x]$.

**(iii)** We call $\gcd(a_0, \dots, a_n)$ a ***content*** of $f(x)$, denoted by $c(f)$ or $c(f(x))$. If $f(x) = c \in D$, then $c(f) := c$.

**(iv)** $f(x)$ is said to be ***primitive*** if $c(f)$ is a unit.

정수에서와 비슷한 센스로 정의하지만 항상 순서 관계를 줄 수 있는 것은 아니다. 때문에 최대공약수의 경우 그 크기가 최대라는 의미보다는 약수의 개수가 최대라는 의미로 이해할 수 있다.

또한 관사에서 알 수 있듯이 일반적인 환의 경우 최대공약수는 유일할 필요도 없고, 항상 존재할 필요도 없다. 그러면 $\gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)$과 같이 기호를 쓸 수가 없는데, 실제로는 단위원을 곱한 경우에 한해서 정의됨을 보일 수 있다. 아래 Remark에 적어둔 것처럼, 최대공약수들은 모두 단위원만큼만 차이가 난다. 예컨대 정수 $3, 6$의 최대공약수는 $3$인데, 정수환에서 단위원은 $1, -1$이므로 일반적으로는 $3$과 $-3$모두 최대공약수로 택할 수 있다는 뜻이다. 그리고 $3$과 $-3$은 단위원 $-1$만큼 차이가 나고, 이 차이만큼 나는 경우를 같은 경우로 본다면 최대공약수 $\gcd(3, 6)$은 잘 정의된다. 같은 맥락에서 content $c(f)$도 잘 정의할 수 있다.

## Remark 2
**(i)** Let $D$ be an integral domain, and let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ be nonzero elements in $D$. Suppose that $\gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ exists. Then $c$ is a gcd of $a_1, \dots, a_n$ $\iff$ $c \sim \gcd(a_1, \dots a_n)$.

**(ii)** Let $D$ be a UFD, and let $f(x)$ be a nonzero polynomial in $D[x]$. Then $c$ is a content of $f(x)$ $\iff$ $c \sim c(f)$.

**(iii)** Let $D$ is a UFD (so also PID), and let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ be nonzero elements in $D$. Then $\gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ exists.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
**(i)** $(\implies)$ Since $c$ is a gcd of $a_1, \dots, a_n$, $c \vert a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$, which means that $c$ is a common divisor. Then we obtain $c \vert \gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)$. Similarly, we have $\gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n) \vert c$, so $c \sim \gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)$.

$(\impliedby)$ Suppose that $c \sim \gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)$. Since $D$ is an integral domain, $c \approx \gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)$. Then $\gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n) = cu$ for some unit $u \in D$. Then $c \vert a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$.

If $r$ is a common divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$, then $r \vert \gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)$. Note that $c = \gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)u^{-1}$. Then 

$$r \vert \gcd(a_1, \dots, a_n)u^{-1} \implies r \vert c.$$

Hence, $c$ is a gcd of $a_1, \dots, a_n$.

**(ii)** It follows directly from **(i)**.

**(iii)** If there is a unit $a_i$ among $a_1, \dots, a_n$, then $a_i$ is a gcd of $a_1, \dots, a_n$.

Suppose that all $a_i$'s are nonunit. Since $D$ is a UFD, each $a_i$ has a finite factorization into irreducible elements, unique up to order and associates. In the factorizations of $a_1, \dots, a_n$, choose one representative from each associate class of irreducible factors and absorb the resulting units into the unit coefficient of each factorization.

If there is no common irreducible divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$, then we will show that $1$ is a gcd of $a_1, \dots, a_n$. If $d$ is a common divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$ which is nonunit, then $d$ has a irreducible facotr $p$. Then $p$ is a common divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$, which is a contradiction. Hence, $d$ is a unit, so $d \vert 1$. Therefore, $1$ is a gcd of $a_1, \dots, a_n$.

Suppose that $a_1, \dots, a_n$ have common irreducible divisors, and let $p_1, \dots p_r$ be all common irreducible divisors of $a_1, \dots, a_n$ which are chosen in the above factorization. Note that $p_i \not \approx p_j, \forall i \neq j$. 

For each $j = 1, \dots, r$, we choose the greatest positive integer $\alpha_j$ such that $p_j^{\alpha_j} \vert a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n\}$. Let

$$d = p_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots p_r^{\alpha_r}.$$

By above construction, $d$ is a common divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$. Let $c$ be a common divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$. If $c$ is a unit, then clearly $c \vert d$. Suppose that $c$ is nonunit, and $p$ is an irreducible factor of $c$. Since $p \vert c$ and $c \vert a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$, $p$ is a common irreducible divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$, which implies that $p \approx p_j$ for some $j \in \{ 1, \dots, r \}$. Hence, we obtain

$$c = up_1^{\beta_1} \cdots p_r^{\beta_r}$$

for some unit $u in D$ and nonnegative integers $\beta_j$ with $0 \le \beta_j \le \alpha_j$ by the maximality of $\alpha_j$. Thus, $c \vert d$, which means that $d$ is a gcd of $a_1, \dots, a_n$. $\blacksquare$
:::

## Theorem 6
Let $D$ be a UFD, and let $f(x), g(x)$ be a nonzero polynomial in $D[x]$.

**(i)** Let $c \in D$. Then $c$ is a content of $f(x)$ $\iff$ $f(x) = cg(x)$ for some primitive polynomial $g(x) \in D[x]$.

**(ii)** **(Gauss's Lemma)** A finite product of primitive polynomials in $D[x]$ is primitive.

**(iii)** $c(fg) \sim c(f)c(g)$.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
**(i)** Write $f(x) = a_0 + \cdots + a_nx^n$.

$(\implies)$ Suppose that $c$ is a content of $f(x)$. Then $a_i = cb_i$ for some $b_i \in D$ for each $i = 0, \dots, n$. Let $g(x) = b_0 + \cdots b_nx^n$. Then $f(x) = cg(x)$. We will show that $g(x)$ is primitive.

Let $d$ be a content of $g(x)$. Then $d \vert b_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$, so $cd \vert a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots n \}$. Since $c$ is a content of $f(x)$, we have $cd \vert c$, so $d$ is a unit. Hence, $g(s)$ is primitive.

$(\impliedby)$ Write $g(x) = b_0 + \cdots + b_nx^n$. Since $f(x) = cg(x)$, we have $a_i = cb_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n\}$, so $c$ is a common divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$.

Let $d$ be a content of $f(x)$. Then $c \vert d$, so $d = cs$ for some $s \in D$. We will show that $s$ is a unit. Note that $d \vert a_i$, so $cs \vert cb_i$. Then $s \vert b_i$, so $s \vert c(g)$. Since $g$ is primitive, $c(g)$ is a unit, which means that $s$ is a unit. Hence, $c \sim d$, so $c$ is a content of $f(x)$.

**(ii)** Let $f_1(x), \dots f_n(x)$ be primitive polynomials in $D[x]$. 

We use induction on $n$. Let $f_1(x) = a_0 + \cdots + a_nx^n$ and $f_2(x) = b_0 + \cdots + b_mx^m$, and let

$$g(x) = f_1(x)f_2(x) = c_0 + \cdots + c_{n+m}x^{n+m}.$$

Suppose that $g(x)$ is not primitive. Then there exists an irreducible element $p$ such that $p \mid c(g)$. Note that $p$ is also a prime element of $D$. Since $f_1(x)$ and $f_2(x)$ are primitive, we can find the least nonnegative integers $r$ and $s$ such that $p \nmid a_r$ and $p \nmid b_s$, which means that $p \mid a_i$ and $p \mid b_j$ for all $i \in \{ 1, \dots, r-1 \}$ and $j \in \{ 1, \dots, s_1 \}$. 

Note that

$$c_{r+s} = (a_0b_{r+s} + \cdots + a_{r-1}b_{s+1}) + a_rb_s + (a_{r+1}b_{s-1} + \cdots + a_{r+s}b_0).$$

Also, note that

$$p \mid (a_0b_{r+s} + \cdots + a_{r-1}b_{s+1}) \quad \text{and} \quad p \mid (a_{r+1}b_{s-1} + \cdots + a_{r+s}b_0).$$

Since $p \mid c_{r+s}$, we must obtain $p \mid a_rb_s$, so $p \mid a_r$ or $p \mid b_s$ because $p$ is a prime element. This is a contradiction to the choice of $r$ and $s$, and therefore $g(x)$ is primitive.

Suppose that the result holds for $n = m$ for some $m \ge 2$. Then $f_1(x) \cdots f_m(x)$ is primitive. Hence, $(f_1(x) \cdots f_m(x))f_{m+1}(x)$ is primitive, and therefore the induction is complete.

**(iii)** First, we prove the case that $g(x)$ is constant, so $g(x) = d \in D$. Let $f(x) = a_0 + \cdots + a_nx^n$. Then $df(x) = da_0 + \cdots + da_nx^n$. Since $c(f) \mid a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$, we have $dc(f) \mid da_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$. Thus, $dc(f) \mid c(df)$.

Note that $d \mid da_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$, so $d \mid c(df)$. Then $c(df) = dt$ for some $t \in D$, so $dt \mid da_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n\}$. Hence, $t \mid a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$, so $dt \mid da_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$. Thus, $c(df) \mid dc(f)$, and therefore $c(df) \sim dc(f)$.

Now, we will show that $c(fg) \sim c(f)c(g)$. By **(i)**, $f(x) = c(f)f_1(x)$ and $g(x) = c(g)g_1(x)$ for some primitive polynomials $f_1(x), g_1(x) \in D[x]$. Then $f(x)g(x) = c(f)c(g)f_1(x)g_1(x)$.

Note that $c(fg) \sim c(f)c(g)c(f_1g_1)$ by the first case. Since $f_1(x), g_1(x)$ is primitive, $f_1(x)g_1(x)$ is also primitive by Gauss's Lemma. Hence, $c(f_1g_1)$ is a unit, so $c(fg) \sim c(f)c(g)$. $\blacksquare$
:::

# Bezout Domain
## Definition 7
An integral domain $D$ is called a ***Bézout domain*** if every finitely generated ideal is principal.

이름부터 딱 베주 항등식과 연관이 있으리라 짐작할 수 있고, 실제로 아래 정리와 같이 정리할 수 있다.

## Theorem
**(i)** An integral domain $D$ is a Bézout domain $\iff$ for nonzero $a_1, \dots, a_n \in D$, there exists a gcd $d$ of $a_1, \dots, a_n$ such that $(d) = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ and $d = a_1b_1 + \cdots + a_nb_n$ for some $b_1, \dots, b_n \in D$. 

**(ii)** Every PID is a Bézout domain.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
### Proof
**(i)** $(\implies)$ Suppose that $D$ is a Bézout domain. Then $(a_1, \dots, a_n) = (d)$ for some $d \in D$. Since $d \in (a_1, \dots, a_n)$, $d = a_1b_1 + \cdots + a_nb_n$ for some $b_1, \dots, b_n \in D$. 

Since $a_i \in (d), \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$, we have $d \mid a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$. Let $c$ be a common divisor of $a_1, \dots, a_n$. Since $c \mid a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n \}$, $(d) = (a_1, \dots, a_n) \subset (c)$, so $c \mid d$. Hence, $d$ is a gcd of $a_1, \dots, a_n$.

$(\impliedby)$ Since $d \mid a_i, \forall i \in \{ 1, \dots, n\}$, we have $(a_1, \dots, a_n) \subset (d)$. Since $d = a_1b_1 + \cdots + a_nb_n$ for some $b_1, \dots, b_n \in D$, $(d) \in (a_1, \dots, a_n)$, so $(a_1, \dots, a_n) = (d)$. Hence, $D$ is Bézout domain.

**(ii)** Let $D$ be a PID. For $a_1, \dots, a_n \in D$, $(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ is an ideal of $D$. Hence, $(a_1, \dots, a_n) = (d)$ for some $d \in D$, and therefore $D$ is a Bézout domain. $\blacksquare$
:::
